articles.title: A 1862 diamond tiara gifted for a French royal wedding disappeared after 1957; nearly 69 years later, the jewel that doubles as a necklace heads to Sotheby’s Geneva to be auctioned for up to $1.3 million
articles.summary: A diamond tiara crafted in 1862 for the London International Exhibition and gifted to a French royal bride two years later is heading to auction at
articles.body: A diamond tiara crafted in 1862 for the London International Exhibition and gifted to a French royal bride two years later is heading to auction at Sotheby’s Geneva. Missing for nearly 69 years, the Mellerio Orléans Tiara, which can also be worn as a necklace, is estimated to fetch up to $1.3 million, according to a report by Town & Country magazine. The European jewel will go under the hammer on November 11 in the auction house’s Royal and Noble Jewels sale, alongside several other pieces, including the tiara worn by the Dowager Duchess of Devonshire at the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.Made in 1862The Mellerio Orléans Tiara dates to around 1862. It was made by Mellerio dits Meller, the oldest jeweller on Place Vendôme in Paris, for the London International Exhibition. It was designed in the Greek Revival style that was popular at the time. The headpiece features a meander pattern, also known as the Greek key design, set with old mine-cut and rose-cut diamonds.Ancient Greek and Roman art influenced the design of the diamond tiara. “This was a direct reflection of Napoleon III’s acquisition of the Campana collection for the Louvre in 1861. The Campana collection was assembled by Giampietro Campana (1809–1880) and encompassed many highly important archaeological finds, including notable ancient jewels. Acquiring part of this collection for the Louvre was an important prestige project for France to establish itself at the vanguard of world culture. Therefore, the timeless Greek key or meander design of the tiara references both classical antiquity and the direct historical context in which it was made, showcasing the glory and prestige of France,” Sotheby’s explains in the listing.The tiara also doubles as a necklace, making it more versatile than most headpieces of its era.A wedding giftTwo years after its London debut, Antoine d’Orléans, Duke of Montpensier, bought the tiara. He gifted it to his eldest daughter, Marie Isabelle, for her wedding to her cousin Philippe d’Orléans (1838–1894), the Count of Paris, in 1864. Philippe was an Orléanist claimant to the French throne. Had the monarchy been restored, Marie Isabelle could have become queen. Instead, the diamonds remained in a family that never sat on the throne.Marie Isabelle died in 1919, and her younger son, Ferdinand, inherited the tiara. He married a Spanish aristocrat in 1923, died two years later and left everything to his wife. She died in 1957. After her death, the family learnt that she had secretly married her personal secretary years earlier and left him her estate. The tiara seems to have vanished around that time. After remaining hidden for decades, it has finally resurfaced. Nobody really knows how.The diamond tiara is heading to auction next month. Sotheby’s has set the estimate at 780,000 to 1,100,000 Swiss francs, or roughly $946,000 to $1.33 million. Prospective buyers should note that these are estimates, not guarantees. They serve as a guide, and results often fall above or below them.Recent Geneva sales show how quickly a royal jewel can exceed its estimate. In May 2021, a natural pearl and diamond tiara linked to the House of Savoy sold for $1.6 million, above its pre-sale estimate of $1 million to $1.5 million, according to a report by National Jeweler. Sotheby’s called it one of the most important tiaras to appear on the market in recent years. The sale next month will reveal whether a piece with a long-hidden past can achieve a similar result.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine got no early warning from partners as Russia hits the power grid again
articles.summary: Russia used ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to launch more attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that Kyiv again received no early warning of the attack from partner countries who in the past have shared that intelligence.
articles.body: Russia used ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to launch more attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that Kyiv again received no early warning of the attack from partner countries who in the past have shared that intelligence. Zelenskyy is grappling with the implications of recent Washington moves benefiting Russian President Vladimir Putin, including waiving U.S. sanctions on Moscow and signing a deal to import Russian diesel. In parallel, limits on Ukraine’s use of the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service have choked Ukrainian drone operations, according to Zelenskyy. Also, a severe shortage of American-made Patriot air defense systems have made Ukraine more vulnerable. Western intelligence sharing has helped Ukraine counter Russia’s devastating ballistic missiles and hold back Moscow’s invasion, which began more than 4 ½ years ago. President Donald Trump says Washington hasn’t stopped providing intelligence to Kyiv, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeated that position Monday. Rubio said he had no information about the previous night’s Russian attack. The Russian nighttime barrage damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities across the country, denying more than a half-million people light, heating and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media. Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the region around it, Zelenskyy said, with officials in the capital reporting that a 21-year-old woman was killed. The Russian Defense Ministry said that it carried out a “massive strike” against targets inside Ukraine, including a data center, a logistics hub storing components for drones and cruise missiles, an industrial facility making drone components, and a locomotive depot where missiles are stored. Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting Russia’s invasion to end. Washington’s efforts to bring peace, meanwhile, have made no progress. Even a recent truce covering energy infrastructure that Trump demanded came to nothing. Western help has been vital for Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s bigger military, but fears have mounted in Kyiv that Trump may be turning his back on Ukraine. Putin, Western analysts and officials say, believes that he can wait for foreign support for Ukraine to unravel and that Russia’s bigger military will then crush Ukraine’s resistance. “Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end. We have responded positively to EVERY ceasefire proposal,” Zelenskyy said Monday on social media. “The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia’s desire to drag this war out.” Ukraine has held back Russia’s bigger army on the front line and has hit back with long-range strikes deep inside Russia that have struck oil refineries and brought fuel shortages. On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St. Petersburg. Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine and torment civilians with drone and missiles strikes that hit trains, shopping malls, gas stations and supermarkets.

articles.body: Why election surveys come with an extra layer of uncertainty. Witnesses recall the horrific scene as a truck plowed through a youth soccer game in Kansas. And inside the silent growth of Flock cameras. Here’s what to know today. Who will actually show up to vote? The question complicating election polls With Democrats favored to win the House and state-level polls showing the Senate within the party’s reach, turnout remains the biggest unknown that will decide what kind of election we have. Republicans are hoping the polls this year are underestimating their support, which has happened in the past. But no one can know for sure who will turn out until after votes are counted — polls aren’t predictions, only snapshots in time. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. National surveys can vary based on how pollsters identify a population that doesn’t yet exist: the “likely voter.” Depending on how we choose to identify likely voters, Democrats have anywhere between a 14- and 4-point advantage over Republicans when it comes to control of Congress. Each firm has its own method, but all likely voter polls rely on two factors: letting the voters tell us what they’ll do, or predicting whether someone will vote based on who they are. Marc Trussler, a senior elections analyst on the NBC News Decision Desk, breaks down how this works using our latest poll as an example. The fight for Congress is playing out largely on Republican-held turf. But headwinds for President Donald Trump’s party have made Democrats optimistic. See the latest data and which states are in play here. Plus, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track,” the highest share yet in Trump’s second term. Witnesses haunted by moment pickup plowed through a Kansas youth soccer game Witnesses of a deadly collision in which a pickup truck barreled through a youth soccer game in Kansas, killing two people and injuring nearly a dozen others, said they are haunted by what they saw and heard. A 6-year-old boy and 35-year-old man were killed in the incident, which unfolded Saturday at a sports complex in Wichita, police said. The driver, 34, was released from custody with a toxicology and mechanical report pending. Erica Case said it was halftime during her son’s soccer game on an adjacent field when she first heard an engine revving, followed by several “boom” sounds. “The moment that I recognized that that wasn’t gunshots, that that was bodies, I lost it,” Case said. “I lost it because it wasn’t just adults. It was also children.” Here’s what others told us. NFL Week 6: The return of Caleb Williams, and life gets worse for the Rams Week 6 of the NFL season featured a star player’s return and another devastating loss for a Super Bowl contender. Here’s all the action you need to know about from yesterday: Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams played for the first time since an injury in Week 2, with a 31-23 victory over the Atlanta Falcons. After entering the season as a Super Bowl favorite, the Los Angeles Rams (2-4) are in last place in the NFC West after an 18-16 loss to the Arizona Cardinals. The Kansas City Chiefs improved to 5-0 with a 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers. Is their offense returning to their dynastic heights?Thanks to familiar miscues, the Dallas Cowboys are off to their worst start in years. Read the full list of takeaways here. Staff Pick: How Flock’s cameras spread through government deals that bypassed public scrutiny I’ve covered Flock Safety’s ALPR cameras for more than a year. These cameras are license plate readers that in many cases create detailed portraits of Americans’ vehicle movements, accessible to police across the country without a warrant. A major part of that story has been how many Americans from multiple walks of life and across the political spectrum have fought back against the cameras in their communities, both legally through their local governments and through illegal vandalism. Over and over, I heard them asking how these cameras, from a company less than a decade old, suddenly went up in their towns and counties, often with their tax dollars and without their knowledge. So I dug into dozens of Flock contracts across the country, and found at least one answer: Many of them were structured in ways that helped reduce how much attention they might get from local communities. In some cases, they would be for amounts just a few dollars shy of a key threshold — like the number that would require a city council to approve them — with local leaders saying outright this was to avoid a vote. In far more cases, I found contracts where Flock helped local officials secure a “no-bid” contract, claiming that their technology was particularly unique and they didn’t have to open up a process of looking at multiple vendors. Flock didn’t invent these tactics, and there’s no indication that they did anything illegal with these contracts. But this survey gives some clear insight into how existing rules communities use for purchasing police tech can help a surveillance tech company quietly install cameras across the country. — Kevin Collier, cyber security reporter Read All About It A service member died after falling during a pregame aerial demonstration at a college football game in San Antonio, Texas.Cindy Crawford has paid tribute to her son Presley Gerber. articles.title: Glendora mayor says he’s ‘outraged’ after serial rapist and Max Factor heir released on parole
articles.summary: The mayor of Glendora is speaking out after Andrew Luster, an heir to the Max Factor cosmetics fortune who was convicted in 2003 on 86 counts of drugging and raping three women, was released to parole supervision last week.
articles.body: The mayor of Glendora is speaking out after Andrew Luster, an heir to the Max Factor cosmetics fortune who was convicted in 2003 on 86 counts of drugging and raping three women, was released to parole supervision last week. “The City of Glendora is beyond disappointed. We are outraged,” Mayor David Fredendall said in a statement Friday. Fredendall said Luster, 62, was released from state prison after serving approximately 20 years and is now reportedly living in the community. NBC Los Angeles has not verified where exactly Luster is living. Luster, the great-grandson of Max Factor, was convicted in 2003 after his capture in Mexico by bounty hunter Duane “Dog” Chapman and returned to Southern California. He was originally handed a 124-year prison sentence, which a Ventura County Superior Court judge vacated in 2013 on the grounds that the trial judge “failed to state specific reasons for imposing full consecutive sentences.” Later that year, his sentence was reduced to 50 years, according to the Ventura County District Attorney’s office. Despite being denied early release on parole multiple times, former Senior Deputy District Attorney Tony Wold, who prosecuted the original case against Luster, said in October 2024 that “even if parole continues to be denied, Luster will be released from prison in approximately two years.” The district attorney’s office said at the time that Luster was scheduled to complete his sentence on Oct. 31 of this year. According to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, he was released on parole on Oct. 11 “after serving his full sentence as required by law.” “This is not an early release,” the CDCR said in a statement Sunday. “According to voter-approved propositions, determinate-sentenced incarcerated individuals may reduce their carceral time due to the earning of worktime and good conduct credits. In this case, Andrew Luster received 977 days of pre-sentence credit and was eligible for credit-earning opportunities while incarcerated.” Fredendall pointed to Proposition 57, approved in 2016, which allows early parole for nonviolent crimes and changed sentence credits and juvenile court decisions, as part of the reason for the release. “The State may argue that this was not technically an early release. It can point to sentencing credits, legal calculations, and administrative requirements,” Fredendall said. “However, those technical explanations do not address the larger concern: how an individual originally sentenced to 124 years in prison for heinous crimes is able to walk out of a secured facility after only 20 years.” Fredendall said the police department will work with state parole authorities to ensure supervision laws and conditions are met, as he demands answers from state lawmakers. “We expect transparency regarding the circumstances of this release, the conditions imposed, and the measures being taken to protect Glendora residents and surrounding communities,” he said. The mayor added that the community stands with the victims. “Their suffering should never be diminished by a system that fails to fully recognize the severity of the crimes committed against them,” Fredendall said. Ann Marie Schubert, former Sacramento County District Attorney and the CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, said California law still treats Luster’s offenses as nonviolent despite repeated attempts to change the law. “The Legislature finally acted in 2024, but for Luster’s victims, it was too late,” Schubert said. “Now a serial rapist is walking free. These women were victimized by Luster and failed repeatedly by a justice system that was supposed to protect them. It’s an absolute travesty of justice. Also to be clear, the law passed was very narrow and did not include rape of an unconscious person.” State Assemblywoman Blanca E. Rubio, who represents the 48th District, also released a statement, saying she is “deeply disturbed” by Luster being released on parole. “This decision raises serious questions about California’s parole system, its accountability, and whether we are truly putting the safety of our communities and the rights of victims first,” her statement read, in part. NBCLA reached out to California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office for a response to Luster’s release.

articles.title: Lula and Bolsonaro trade barbs in Brazil election debate
articles.summary: The race heats up just days before the run-off between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing challenger.
articles.body:
Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.

Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters.

But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.

In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula.

Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.

Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election.

The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.

Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time".

Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.

Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments.

"The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."

Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin".

Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.

Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.

One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.

Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia".

Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."

He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt).

"Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese.

Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power.

He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".

Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".

articles.title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
articles.summary: The 51-year-old faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
articles.body:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.

In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs."

A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.

The woman is the third complainant the jury have heard from in the trial - and the second to allege rape.

The pair had been attending a birthday party in Soho in London in 2004 when the alleged incidents happened.

She said after the alleged sexual assault, "The visual I remember is just this big grin - it felt like a clown, (with) that sort of weird look in the eye. It was a normal conversation about him being on Big Brother. He just moved towards (me) and grabbed both my boobs".

She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock".

"The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said.

"Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

"I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.

After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."

Russell Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

articles.title: Victoria’s Secret reboots its fantasy with a $50M diamond bra
articles.summary: For a brand emerging from a rocky few years, it read as a defiant investment into its own fantasy.
articles.body: On Sunday night, just when you thought the megawatt spectacle that is the Victoria’s Secret runway show couldn’t get any glitzier, out struts Kylie Jenner in a $50 million diamond brasserie. The “Fantasy Bra” is a Victoria’s Secret signature stunt — since 1996, the lingerie brand has designed roughly one bejeweled push-up bra per year, primarily for elevating catwalks. Claudia Schiffer was the first model to wear a Fantasy Bra in a photo shoot, while the last was Elsa Hosk on the runway in 2018 — both were valued at the time at a comparatively modest $1 million. This year, the price tag of previous versions was dwarfed by Jacob & Co.’s $50 million creation. The luxury jewelers engineered Jenner’s bustier out of 91 large white diamonds ranging at between 5 and 18 carats each. At the bra’s center sat one yellow diamond over 75 carats. For a brand emerging from a rocky few years of public criticism and revenue losses, it read as a defiant investment into its own fantasy. Celebrities from Timothée Chalamet and Kris Jenner to Nicole Kidman and Dylan Sprouse watched the procession of familiar Victoria’s Secret Angels such as Joan Smalls and Candice Swanepoel, as well as newer recruits like Paloma Elsesser and Alex Consani. Model Bella Hadid opened the show with a pair of delicate floral wings that looked more comfortable than those of previous shows. “The wings are so much lighter this year, so the girls are really walking,” said Consani backstage. Models strutted in a range of sheer to sportier takes on lingerie, soundtracked to live performances from global girl group Katseye, rapper Megan Thee Stallion and pop singer Tate McRae. Solange Omon was unveiled as the winner of “Angels Among Us” — Victoria’s Secret new social-first reality show posted on YouTube in the weeks leading up to the event. The “America’s Next Top Model”-style series, spearheaded by the brand’s new chief creative officer Adam Selman, captures an ambitious open casting call process to recruit just one model. The competition begins in malls across the US, with thousands lining up to have their runway walk judged by a panel including Selman, Elsesser, Ashley Graham and Gigi Hadid. It’s clear that public appeal towards the brand remains — aside from the staggering number of applicants, the first episode, posted two weeks ago, has over 5 million views. Since his appointment in April 2025, part of Selman’s job has been to contend with the controversial legacy of Victoria’s Secret. Links to Jeffrey Epstein sullied the brand’s reputation, while existential questions over whether its lingerie runway shows — which have been going since 1995, aside from a 6-year hiatus starting in 2019 — are patriarchal or empowering resurface each year like clockwork. In its official comeback show in 2024, before Selman joined, the brand attempted a quick course correct after decades of promoting one body type in the interest of “fantasy.” Plus-size and transgender models were cast for the first time in Victoria’s Secret history, though many called it tokenistic and “woke-washing.” At the beginning of 2026, the brand’s CEO Hillary Super told Fortune it has a commitment to diversity “without being performative, where we have to check every box.” The balancing act seemed to have worked — earlier this summer, the company doubled its share price on the stock market, according to Fortune. For his second Victoria’s Secret runway show, Selman is continuing to toe that line between brand heritage and contemporary attitudes, embracing the fact that it appears the sex-appeal, the glamour, the fantasy, is in some ways, still what people want. His next generation Angels (Graham, Elsesser, Consani, Omon) walk alongside those such as veteran catwalker Adriana Lima, who racked up her 21st show for the brand Sunday night. articles.title: Al Jazeera investigation challenges Israeli account of Heidi Levine attack
articles.summary: Analysis of map coordinates and timelines raises doubts over official Israeli accounts of West Bank settler pogrom.
articles.body:
An Al Jazeera investigation has challenged official Israeli narratives regarding an attack by settlers on Palestinian olive harvesters and an American photojournalist on Friday in Khirbet Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.

The investigation by Al Jazeera’s Data Journalism Unit used open-source verification and analysis of visual and geographic evidence.

Official Israeli accounts of what happened differ: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office has questioned whether Israeli settlers were to blame at all, while the Israeli army has suggested that the military was engaged in addressing a confrontation between Palestinians and settlers at the time.

But verified footage and mapped coordinates reveal a coordinated attack by masked settlers, with Israeli military vehicles passing by shortly before the incident, without intervening.

The October 16 pogrom left veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, with a broken rib, four fractured vertebrae, and wounds requiring hand surgery, despite wearing a clearly marked press vest.

To establish the facts, the Data Journalism Unit monitored and analysed more than 20 videos and photos taken by journalists and witnesses on the ground. The team independently verified the footage, arranged it chronologically, communicated with local journalists, and mapped key locations.

Geospatial analysis pinpoints the settler outpost where the attackers originated, the harvesting land, and the location of the assault on Levine.

The attack on Levine was mapped at the coordinates 32°01’13.5″N 35°18’40.7″E. This site is approximately 455 metres southwest of an outpost on a hill near the Misholash settlement, and just 120 metres north of the land where Palestinians were picking olives.

The unit also identified rooms traditionally used by Palestinians to store fertiliser and agricultural tools, and where farmers occasionally spend the night. These rooms are near the outpost, 430 and 500 metres northeast of the attack site. A local journalist, speaking on condition of anonymity due to security concerns, said that Palestinian owners can no longer enter these rooms, where settlers now stay and gather.

The journalist explained that the outpost is located in Area B under the Oslo Accords, where the Palestinian Authority (PA) manages civil affairs and Israel retains security control. While only a few settlers typically reside in the outpost to “prove” their presence, during any incident, 50 to 100 settlers from other outposts gather there before descending on the fields.

He noted that other settler tents on the adjacent mountain overlooking the village serve as additional gathering points to attack anyone harvesting olives.

Tracking the footage chronologically reveals a gradual escalation leading up to the attack.

Movements began around 8am when a 4×4 vehicle carrying settlers headed towards the site, followed by six motorcycles moving towards the area opposite the harvesters. In a video posted shortly after 9am, about 30 settlers are seen gathering near the farmers.

Al Jazeera correspondent Tharwat Shaqra, who was at the scene, said that Israeli military vehicles passed through the area, and after their passage, settlers headed towards the journalists and farmers, “as if it were a green light.” Independent Israeli journalist Oren Ziv noted that military jeeps made no attempt to stop the masked men.

The settlers then set fire to the olive trees and advanced towards the harvesters, prompting village youths to respond by throwing stones.

Footage subsequently documents the assault on Levine after she was knocked down. Her colleagues could only reach her after young Palestinians pushed the settlers back by throwing stones in their direction.

American journalist Jasper Nathaniel, who helped pull her away, wrote on X: “The only reason I was able to get to Heidi is because Palestinian youth provided cover with stones facing settlers and soldiers with machine guns and tear gas.” He added that the army pursued the young Palestinians after the attack, not the settlers.

During the same period, a video captured the sound of four gunshots followed by two more, which Tharwat Shaqra confirmed originated from the settlers.

Israeli forces only appeared to be deployed at the attack site in later footage, with their vehicles stationed in the settlers’ area. Soldiers then shot local council member Abdel Jaber Obeid and intercepted the ambulance before his transfer to hospital, as the army continued firing tear gas at the olive harvesters.

The timeline and geographical data contradict the official Israeli narratives.

The Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said that “the facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation”. It cited reports indicating “some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths”.

However, footage and testimonies show that the settlers gathered, descended, and burned trees before the youths responded, and the assault on Levine is documented on video.

Conversely, the army did not question the assault, acknowledging the injury of a foreign journalist. The Israeli military stated that forces were dispatched “following a report of a violent confrontation” and broke it up using “riot dispersal means”. It said soldiers “fired warning shots into the air and then fired toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object,” making no mention of the settlers or their gunfire.

The Israeli military’s international spokesperson Ariella Mazor told The Washington Post that soldiers in the area were trying to disperse a large, violent crowd and did not see the assault on Levine.

But evidence from videos and other testimony suggests that military vehicles in the area passed by the settlers without intervening and that Israeli forces eventually directed tear gas at Palestinians after the attack.

The attack prompted widespread condemnation. United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee demanded that “those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison”.

He said that “attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”.

articles.title: Priest killed by falling crucifix during live streamed Mass
articles.summary: A priest has been killed by a falling crucifix at a church in Ecuador as he performed a mass that was being live streamed online.
articles.body: A priest has been killed by a falling crucifix at a church in Ecuador as he performed a mass that was being live streamed online. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died on Saturday at the Perpetuo Socorro church in the city of Guayaquil, southern Ecuador, according to a statement from the city’s archdiocese, published on Facebook on Monday. Video of the incident shows Sánchez leading the mass when a large wooden cross that was standing on the altar behind him falls over and hits him on the head. Shouting can be heard from the congregation, and several people enter the frame and rush toward the priest. On Sunday, the church held a eucharist in memory of Sánchez, led by Cardinal Luis Cabrera, archbishop of Guayaquil. “We are grateful for all of the condolences from around the world, and especially for your prayers for the eternal rest of the soul of Patricio Sánchez,” the statement reads. According to CNN affiliate Ecuavisa, the priest was preparing to lead a wedding ceremony when the tragedy occurred. Police have not commented on the incident so far, Ecuavisa reported. CNN has reached out to the Archdiocese of Guayaquil for comment.

articles.body:
President Trump is defending his decision to delay new sanctions on Russia, arguing he does not want to drive Moscow away from the negotiating table as he works to end the war in Ukraine.

The move, however, is drawing increasing scrutiny from Republicans. Sens. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) have been the most vocal in recent days, pushing for the administration to reenforce the penalties under legislation named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the weekend addressed economic fallout from the war in Iran, saying the trajectory of oil prices will depend on how the conflict unfolds.

Meanwhile, with just two weeks until the midterms , Republicans are fighting to maintain control of Congress despite faring poorly in recent polling.

Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon on Sunday defended her call for GOP Sen. Ashley Moody (Fla.) to be jailed over allegations of fraud. In the Texas Senate race, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), whose faltering campaign has rattled Republicans .

Trump will sign an executive order with first lady Melania Trump in the Rose Garden Tuesday morning. Later, the president continues his campaign blitz in Park City, Kan., while Vice President Vance travels to Hendersonville, N.C.
